bib.title: TurboTransformers: An Efficient GPU Serving System For Transformer Models

question: How can transformer models be served on GPUs with low latency and high throughput when computation is heavy and input length varies per request?
hypothesis: A variable-length-aware runtime (fused kernels, faster batch reductions, graph-aware chunk allocator) plus a DP batch scheduler beats fixed-length-oriented runtimes and naive batching on variable-length workloads.
contributions: A new parallel algorithm for batch reduction kernels like Softmax and LayerNorm on GPU
A sequence-length-aware memory allocation algorithm using the computation graph
A sequence-length-aware batch scheduler using dynamic programming to reach optimal throughput

method.summary: A C++/Python GPU runtime fuses non-GEMM kernels between GEMMs, uses a multi-element warp reduction for Softmax/LayerNorm, and a chunk-based allocator that computes tensor offsets from the graph once the sequence length is known. A serving framework (message queue, response cache, batch scheduler) sorts queued requests by length and picks batch boundaries by dynamic programming over a measured cost table.
method.task: transformer inference serving (BERT-style classification, Seq2seq translation decoder)

datasets.name: Randomly generated texts
datasets.split: BERT/Albert/DistilBert lengths uniform 5-500; Decoder Chinese texts length 28-137; serving workloads length uniform 2-100 and 5-500
datasets.source: randomly generated/sampled; same random seed across tests

models.name: Bert (base)
models.hidden: 4096 (as printed in Table 3; likely a typo for base BERT)

inference.decoding: Seq2Seq decoder beam_size=4, max_target_len=500; otherwise not stated
inference.samples: Runtime: sequential execution of randomly generated requests of different lengths, one run, same seed across systems; number of repetitions not stated. Serving: Poisson arrivals at 20-1500 req/sec; duration not stated.

parameters.batch_scheduler: hungry strategy, max batch size 20; lazy alternative uses timeout and max batch size and fires if wait plus estimated latency exceeds half the latency constraint
parameters.cached_cost: warmup over all (seq len, batch size) takes tens of minutes; large spaces sampled and interpolated
parameters.allocator: chunk 2MB, K_SCALE 1.2, unused chunks released after each inference
parameters.Tensor Core: on for Turbo-TC and for the 5-500 serving experiment

other.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X CPU and one RTX 2060 GPU (kernel speedups Fig 5 on Tesla V100; profiling motivations on V100 and M40)

metrics.name: Serving throughput
metrics.definition: responses per second at which service saturates (critical point where request and serving throughput are equal)

metrics.name: Memory footprint
metrics.definition: intermediate tensor footprint; peak GPU memory by nvidia-smi sampled every 1 ms

eval.protocol: Single machine, random inputs with fixed seed; no variance, repeats or significance tests reported. Accuracy not evaluated except the claim of minimal precision loss for Tensor Core.

availability.data: inputs randomly generated by benchmark scripts

results.claim: Serving throughput at saturation: PyTorch no batching vs Turbo with DP batch scheduler, lengths 2-100
results.setup: BERT classification service, RTX 2060, Poisson arrivals, lengths uniform 2-100, hungry strategy, max batch 20, cache off
results.quote: The serving throughput of PyTorch-Nobatch is saturated at 99 resp/sec. The serving throughput of Turbo-NoBatch is saturated at 237 resp/sec (2.39x). Turbo-Naive-Batch improves it to 323 resp/sec (3.26x) and the Turbo-DP-Batch futher improves it to 402 resp/sec (4.06x).

results.claim: Serving throughput at saturation with lengths 5-500 and Tensor Cores: Turbo-TC-DP-Batch vs PyTorch-NoBatch
results.setup: BERT service, RTX 2060, lengths uniform 5-500, Tensor Core on, max batch 20
results.quote: Turbo-TC-DP-Batch further improves it to 144 resp/sec (2.4x).

results.claim: Naive batching hurts on widely varying lengths: worse than no batching at 5-500
results.setup: BERT service, RTX 2060, lengths 5-500, Turbo-TC-Naive-Batch
results.quote: Due to the additional zero-padding overhead, Turbo-TC-Naive-Batch's throughput is 98 resp/sec, which is even worse than Turbo-NoBatch.

results.claim: DP scheduler improves worked example throughput by 35% (five requests 17,18,52,63,77)
results.setup: Illustrative example, base BERT; 3 batches vs 1 batch of 5 (20.62 ms vs 15.24 ms in Fig 8)
results.quote: As shown in Figure 8, the response throughput (resp/sec) improved 35% by the optimal scheduling scheme.

results.claim: Average runtime speedup over PyTorch on fixed-length BERT
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060, batch sizes 1 and 20, seq lengths 10-500; range 1.23x-2.77x
results.quote: Compared with PyTorch, the speedup of Turbo is 1.23x-2.77x, on average 1.54x.

results.claim: Average speedup over PyTorch on variable-length BERT
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060, random lengths 5-500; range 0.97x-2.44x; gains larger on short inputs
results.quote: In the case of Bert inference, Turbo's speedups to PyTorch are ranging from 0.97x-2.44x, on average 1.25x.

results.claim: Average speedup over onnxruntime on variable-length BERT is about parity
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060, random lengths 5-500; range 0.88x-1.05x
results.quote: In the case of Bert, the speedups of Turbo to onnxruntime are ranging from 0.88x-1.05x, on average 1.01x.

results.claim: On fixed-length BERT, Turbo is on average slower than TensorRT
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060, speedup of Turbo vs TensorRT 5.1.5, range 0.53x-0.96x; TensorRT uses offline tuning
results.quote: Compared with TensorRT, the speedup of Turbo is 0.53x-0.96x, on average 0.87x.

results.claim: On fixed-length BERT, Turbo is on average slightly slower than FasterTransformer
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060, FasterTransformer v1, range 0.71x-1.32x
results.quote: Compared with Faster Transformers, the speedup of Turbo is 0.71x-1.32x, on average 0.91x.

results.claim: Peak GPU memory of Turbo vs PyTorch and onnxruntime
results.setup: BERT, lengths random, nvidia-smi sampled every 1 ms, includes CUDA context
results.quote: the peak GPU memory used for Turbo is 663 MB while the GPU peak memory used by PyTorch is 1307 MB and 1653 MB for onnxruntime.

results.claim: Max intermediate-tensor memory of Turbo allocator
results.setup: BERT, random lengths 5-500, C++ API; close to GSOC; PyTorch/onnxruntime caches grow and never shrink after a length-460 request
results.quote: the maximum memory usage of us is 12.15 MB.

results.claim: Allocator offset-scheduling overhead as share of inference latency
results.setup: BERT, random lengths 5-500; range 0.07%-5.77%
results.quote: the average cost of offset scheduling (cost of Algorithm 1) is 1.8% on average (0.07%-5.77%) of DNN inference latency.

results.claim: PyTorch BERT spends 38.2% of time in non-GEMM kernels at large batch
results.setup: Tesla V100, BERT, batch 20, seq len 128
results.quote: only 61.8% of the time is spent on GEMM kernels, and 38.2% is spent on non-GEMM intensive cores

results.claim: PyTorch leaves the GPU idle 80.64% of the time at batch 1, seq len 40
results.setup: Tesla V100, BERT, batch 1, seq len 40 (kernel launch overhead)
results.quote: GPU is completely idle 80.64% of the time.

results.claim: Softmax share of attention time before optimizing at batch 20 seq 500
results.setup: PyTorch Softmax measured vs attention with our runtime; after optimization 15.46%
results.note: Table 2 cells; after-values 15.46%; LayerNorm 83.38% before, 4.24% after
results.where: p4 Table 2 row Softmax/Attention before, column (20, 500)

results.claim: Allocation waits idle: 50% of compute idle on Tesla M40 when allocating on demand
results.setup: Tesla M40, batch 20, seq len 128
results.quote: 50% of the computing resources idle wait for memory allocation ready on Tesla M40 (batch size = 20, sequence length = 128)

results.claim: GEMM share of Turbo BERT time at seq 20 and 400
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060; GEMM 82.80% at seq 400; Softmax 1.85%/4.57%; LayerNorm 2.71%/3.64%
results.quote: In the sequence length 20, the GEMM kernels account for 70.31% of overall computation time.

results.claim: Average Albert speedup over PyTorch is smaller because GEMM dominates
results.setup: Albert (large config), RTX 2060, lengths 5-500; range 1.04x-1.45x
results.quote: In Albert inference, Turbo's speedups to PyTorch are ranging from 1.04x-1.45x, on average 1.17x.

results.claim: Decoder average speedup over PyTorch
results.setup: Seq2Seq decoder, RTX 2060, source length 28-137; range 1.14x-1.20x
results.quote: In the case of Decoder inference, Turbo's speedups to PyTorch are ranging from 1.14x-1.20x, on average 1.16x.

results.claim: Latency at saturation under DP batching: avg latency 24.74 ms at 402 req/sec; DP raises long-request latency vs naive batching at 2-100
results.setup: BERT, RTX 2060, lengths 2-100, Turbo-DP-Batch avg latency at 402 req/sec (min 4.23, max 57.02)
results.quote: Turbo-DP-Batch sorts the requests in MQ, the execution of long sequences is delayed, thus increasing their latency.

limits: All experiments run on a single consumer RTX 2060 (plus V100/M40 for motivating profiles); no data-center GPU serving numbers for the end-to-end systems.
Workloads are randomly generated texts with uniform length distributions; real traffic length distributions, SLO tail latencies (p99) and accuracy are not evaluated.
No repeats, variance or significance tests; PyTorch 1.5 / onnxruntime 1.3 / TensorRT 5.1.5 versions are dated.
GEMM is not optimized, so long sequences gain little; runtime is about 10% slower than FasterTransformer and TensorRT on fixed-length input.
DP scheduler reorders requests, delaying long ones; needs a warmup cost table taking tens of minutes, assumes load balancer keeps servers within SLO.
Encoder and small decoder models only; no autoregressive LLM serving, KV cache or continuous batching.
Table 3 hidden_size values (4096 for Bert) look inconsistent with base BERT.
